cards.title: Four-pronged buyer research methodology
cards.summary: Combine qualitative customer conversations, quantitative surveys, digital intelligence tools and social listening to answer who your buyers are, how they behave and why.
cards.use_when: You need to build or rebuild buyer personas and want evidence-based insights rather than assumptions or template personas.
steps: Run qualitative customer conversations first (about 20 x 30-minute calls) to surface the buyer's why, trigger moment, journey, pain points and emotional drivers.
Design a quantitative survey to verify the interview trends at scale and to collect data-centric attributes that are easier to capture in a form (role, company size, years in role).

Use digital intelligence tools (for the source: SparkToro, Audience, IBM Watson-based data) to see how the wider audience actually behaves: platforms they use, influencers who shape buying decisions, and buying mindset (e.g. move fast vs needs a sales team, risk-taker vs conservative, self-serve vs wants support).
Run social listening (source used Brand24) to track topics and pain points people discuss, not to monitor your own brand mentions.
Compile all four data sets, then segment the personas by jobs to be done rather than by age, gender or job title.
Use the digital data for how people behave and the conversations for why they behave that way; cross-check what people say against what the tools show they do.
caveats: The four-prong framework is universal in the source's view, but the number of personas and specific data points gathered are not universal and should match the business.
Digital tools show behavior but never explain motivation; conversations explain motivation but can be inaccurate about behavior.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Run 30-minute discovery calls, not sales calls
cards.summary: Frame customer interviews explicitly as exploratory conversations about the buyer's experience to fill your calendar and avoid the demo/upsell fear.
cards.use_when: Recruiting and conducting customer interviews to extract buyer insights for personas, messaging or product decisions.
steps: State clearly up front (in the scheduling email and at the start of the call) that you are not a product expert, cannot solve their problem, and are not there to demo or upsell.
Tell them exactly what the call is about and how much time you need (source uses 30 minutes) so there is no confusion or concern about a hidden sales motive.
Ask about their full customer journey: how they found the product, why they use it, their experience and emotions around it.
Aim for about 20 conversations; the source cites Nielsen/company research (via Deploy Empathy by Michele Hansen) that 20 conversations yield about 97% sentiment coverage of the audience.
Expect customers who love or hate the product to want to talk; if few people will book, that itself signals weak feeling toward the product.
caveats: The 97% figure is a cited research claim, not a guarantee for every audience.
Fear of bothering customers or triggering cancellations is largely unfounded per the source's experience, but interviews should still be handled with care.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Incentivize hard-to-reach interview participants
cards.summary: Match the incentive to the participant's status: product perks for normal customers, charitable donations for busy executives.
cards.use_when: Recruiting interviews with customers who are hard to book, especially senior or high-earning buyers.
steps: For regular customers, offer low-cost brand-relevant perks: a company t-shirt for signing up, or early/beta access to a new tool (source example: three months of beta access).
For busy founders, CEOs or difficult audiences, donate a set amount to a charity of their choice in their name rather than paying them (source used $30 for 30 minutes).
Avoid offering cash to people whose time is worth far more than the amount; it creates an awkward business transaction and cheapens the ask.
Use the charitable framing as a favor exchange that attracts the right caliber of participant without quantifying their time.
caveats: Incentive type and amount are examples, not benchmarks; calibrate to the audience.
Confirm any tool or platform perks are still offered before promising them.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Segment personas by jobs to be done, not demographics
cards.summary: Group buyers by the job they are trying to accomplish and the trigger that makes them buy, which produces stronger segmentation than age, gender or job title.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to structure buyer personas or audience segments for campaigns, product and strategy.
steps: Reject purely demographic groupings (age, gender, favorite color, grocery store) because they do not help you write copy or make product decisions.
Identify the job the buyer is trying to get done and the trigger moment that causes them to start looking for a solution.
Group people who share the same job and trigger into one persona, even if their titles or demographics differ.
Write the persona so it can serve marketing, product, sales and customer success, not just one campaign.
Every persona should contain evidence, trigger moments and a job statement.
caveats: The number of personas is not universal; scope varies by business.
Some marketers insist a persona must follow the traditional named/acronym format; the source treats naming as optional and argues the job-based insight matters more.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Avoid the dusty, unused persona trap
cards.summary: Most marketers create personas but never use them; build documentation that is actually referenced for campaigns, product and strategy.
cards.use_when: Auditing or replacing an existing persona doc that is not used in go-to-market work.
steps: Check whether the current persona is referenced in campaign launches, product launches, copy or strategy; if not, treat it as a check-the-box artifact.
Replace fluff (fictional names, stock photos, lifestyle details like shops at Trader Joe's) with buyer insights: concerns, product-related jobs, objections and trigger moments.
Call the output whatever the team will accept (buyer persona, buyer insights, buyer documentation) as long as the content is useful.
Distribute the persona across marketing, product, sales and customer success so the research investment pays off in multiple functions.
caveats: Citing the source's survey via Audience: roughly 90%+ of marketers create personas, but about 77% never use them for a launch or copy; these are reported figures, not guarantees.
Naming conventions are contentious; do not force one if it blocks adoption.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Use surveys to verify interviews and capture data-centric attributes
cards.summary: Design a survey after interviews to confirm trends at scale and collect structured facts that work better in a form than in conversation.
cards.use_when: You have preliminary interview insights and want to validate them across a larger audience.
steps: Develop the survey questions after analyzing interview themes, focusing on what needs verification at scale.
Include structured, factual items that are easier to answer in a form: role, tenure with the company, number of employees, buying authority, and similar data-centric fields.
Use the survey to confirm or challenge the qualitative trends rather than to discover entirely new motivations.
Combine survey results with conversations, digital intelligence and social listening before forming personas.
caveats: Surveys are better for facts and scale than for uncovering deep motivation; keep them complementary to interviews.
Question and sample design still affect validity; do not treat survey output as automatically representative.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Social listening for pain-point topics, not brand mentions
cards.summary: Track what people say about problems and frustrations rather than your brand so personas reflect real language and concerns.
cards.use_when: Adding a social listening layer to persona research or messaging development.
steps: Set up a listening tool (source used Brand24; verify current alternatives and interfaces).
Monitor the topics and pain points relevant to your category, not brand handles or mentions, because the goal is audience context rather than community management.
Capture how people describe frustrations and objections in their own words for use in copy and messaging.
Use listening data to fact-check interview themes and to gauge whether interviewees' descriptions match broader public conversation.
caveats: Listening provides background and validation, not the why behind individual behavior; that still comes from conversations.
Tool capabilities and pricing change; confirm before committing.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Use digital intelligence to see how buyers actually behave
cards.summary: Digital intelligence tools reveal platforms, influencers and buying mindsets of the wider audience, filling in behavior that interviews cannot reliably capture.
cards.use_when: You need audience behavior, channel and buying-mindset data to complement interviews and surveys.
steps: Use audience research tools (source used SparkToro and Audience) to see where the broader audience spends time and which platforms they use most.
Identify influencers who shape their decisions, both on social media and in buying contexts.
Assess buying mindset: do they purchase quickly, prefer self-serve, or require a sales team; are they risk-takers or conservative; do they want help or figure it out alone.
Layer in psychographic or socio-emotional data where available (source cites IBM Watson-based data) to understand risk tolerance and support preferences.
Combine these behavioral signals with conversation insights to complete the picture.
caveats: Behaviors seen in tools can be wrong or incomplete; treat them as directional.
Tool availability and data sources change; verify current capabilities.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Ask churned customers why they left
cards.summary: Direct outreach to churning customers reveals fixable reasons and can be acted on quickly, as in the subscription chicken-box example.
cards.use_when: Retention is slipping or cancellation rates are rising, especially when paid acquisition is getting harder.
steps: Identify customers who are leaving or have recently cancelled.
Ask them directly why they are leaving instead of inferring from usage data alone.
Act on the specific reported reasons (the source's example: a live chat option on the site).
Keep this as an ongoing practice, not a one-time investigation.
caveats: The chicken-box example is anecdotal and illustrative, not a benchmark.
Some reasons will be outside your control; separate fixable from non-fixable causes.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Talk to first customers and keep it in your culture
cards.summary: Regardless of business type, understand what you solve for customers and keep talking to buyers from day one instead of stopping after launch.
cards.use_when: Starting or scaling any business and deciding whether to institutionalize customer conversations.
steps: Figure out exactly why customers purchase; do not assume you already know.
Talk to your very first buyers and treat the conversations as exploratory, not as demos or upgrades.
Make customer conversations a permanent part of company culture rather than a one-time research phase.
Push different functions (marketing, support, sales) into customer calls so they understand what is being solved and can feed insight back into the business.
caveats: The source frames this as universally applicable (plumber, farm, B2B SaaS, DTC), but execution details differ by business.
Do not let the practice become a disguised sales call, which defeats the purpose.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Cross-check what people say against what they do
cards.summary: Conversations reveal the why of behavior but people can misreport what they do; digital intelligence and listening data show actual behavior.
cards.use_when: Reconciling conflicting evidence between interviews and analytics/listening data, or designing research to minimize blind spots.
steps: Get motivation and the why from conversations, since digital tools will never explain motivation.
Get how people actually behave from digital intelligence, since people can misreport their own behavior.
Triangulate across all four data sources (conversations, surveys, digital intelligence, social listening) before committing to persona conclusions.
Expect mismatch between stated and observed behavior and treat it as signal rather than error.
caveats: No single data source is authoritative; triangulation is the point.
Source frames this as a cognitive bias problem: people describe what they think they do.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx

cards.title: Apply jobs-to-be-done using the milkshake story
cards.summary: The milkshake case is a compact way to explain JTBD to clients and teams before applying it to their business.
cards.use_when: Introducing jobs-to-be-done to a client or internal team that has not encountered it.
steps: Tell the milkshake example: intuition says people buy milkshakes for a sweet tooth, but the job was a clean, easy on-the-go snack.
Use it to show that the reason for purchase is often different from the obvious assumption.
Then translate the same reasoning to the client's product: what job is the buyer hiring it to do, and in what situation?
Use the story as a bridge before presenting persona or JTBD findings.
caveats: The story is illustrative; it does not itself produce the client's jobs.
The source notes clients often know the milkshake story but still need help applying JTBD to their own context.
cards.source_name: _Adrienne Barnes on Best Buyer Personas, Marketing & Motherhood.docx
